No. 58, after Hiroshige (複製：大はしあたけの夕立・ 広重後 Fukusei：Ōhashi Atake no yūdachi・Hiroshige no ato)
Utagawa Hiroshige 歌川広重 (1797-1858) - after the artist

An undated (c. 1930s) small format reproduction after Hiroshige's 1857 Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge at Atake, No. 58 from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. The original print has been called the "undisputed masterpiece" of the series.
The publisher of this print was Yokohama-based Hideo Takemura (H. Takemura & Co.) who targeted his work at a Western audience, specializing in, as printed on his business card, Christmas Cards, Japanese Old Colour Prints, Famous Modern Colour Prints and Water Colors.
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (Doi Hangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

After: Shrine by the River by Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki)

After Shōtei's small format print Shrine by the River originally published by Watanabe Shōzaburō (1885-1962) in 1936. The unidentified artist who created this collection's print, published by an unnamed publisher, has taken the background from Shōtei's print and substituted a new foreground. Watanabe became so concerned about Shōtei's designs being copied that he put the following notice into his 1936 catalogue:
About "Copyright"
"At the same time an artist draws a certain atmosphere, there are created copyright and right of personality as in the case of an author. The right of personality should not be infringed by other people and is not transferrable. It lasts as long as an artist lives, while the copyright is a transferable property.
"In case any picture already issued reproduced or copied by the third person without permission, he will be sued and judged as a violation of copyright, that is, as the infringement of property right.
"There had been examples that a few pictures issued by my shop were reproduced or copied without permission previous to the Great Earthquake disaster [1923] and after it. On each occasion the violator had to pay damages and to write letters of apology.
"As said above, the copyright is well protected with the right of the artist's personality according to the copyright law."

One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the making of sanbon (highly refined sugar) in Sanuki Province, present day Kagawa Prefecture.
Sanuki (讃岐国) was an old province of Japan on the island of Shikoku, with the same boundaries as modern Kagawa Prefecture. It faced the Inland Sea and bordered on Awa and Iyo Provinces. Across Naruto strait it bordered Awaji Province too.
Basil Hall Chamberlain, British Japanologist, in his 1907 Handbook for Travellers in Japan, notes that "The chief production of this province of Sanuki are popularly known as ‘the three white things’ (sam-paku), viz, salt, sugar, and cotton. The sugar industry is modern, having been introduced from Satsuma only half a century ago."

Five male machinists at work on their lathes in this sixteenth print from the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1. This print is one of a small number of prints in the series depicting modern industry in Japan.
A translated version of the original Japanese language commentary accompanying this print reads, "A machine is formed by a collection of parts. The more complex the individual parts are, the more sophisticated the machine and its function. Nowadays, compared to a carpenter and a potter, the machinist has already become a major occupation. As a major role in heavy industry, light industry, and precision machinery industry, everyone agrees that this profession is a vital cornerstone. There is no doubt that this profession, which requires extraordinary skill instead of manpower, is extremely popular in today's world."[1]

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]

[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 14.
[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1 (昭和職業繪盡 第一輯 Shōwa shokugyō e-zukushi daiishū)
December 1954 Shōwa 29, 12th month - as printed in Japanese in the left margin.

Wada presents us with his rendition of shoe shiners at work in a park-like setting on a sunny day in this 4th print in the twenty-four print post-WWII series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, Continued" (3rd series). The happy picture that Wada presents us with is a much prettier picture than reality. Finding work in the aftermath of the war was tough, especially for veterans many of whom were forced to take this type of labor to survive. Disadvantaged boys also worked shining shoes to survive.
The English language commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "'Shoe-Shine' became so popular in Japan after the war, that the 'shoe-shine boy' became the title of a hit song. Shoe-shine seems now to have become a legal occupation for men, and is a business conducted on the streets of Japan. Originally most Japanese thought it was rather a luxurious service, and a waste of money and time. After the war many people began to wear well-polished shoes as they came to afford well pressed white shirts. I am told that Spain is famous for this skill, and there are many shoe-shiners in its big cities, but this does not mean that all Spanish men are beaus. It seems to me that this profession may be considered as one of the solutions for unemployment. [I do not have much interest in this, so I am not very sure, but it seems.] Shoe-shiners are making their own efforts to make all shoes shine beautifully. Some of them have actually achieved a technique like a craftsman."

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES, CONTINUED (3RD SERIES)
After WWII, the publisher Shinagawa Kyoomi issued the third set of prints in the popular pre-war series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures." His former publishing business, Nishinomiya Shoin, being destroyed during WWII, Shinagawa opened a new publishing business in Kyoto, Kyōto Hangain 京都版画院. At first, Kyōto Hangain published re-prints from the pre-war series 1 and 2 of “Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures,” but would go on to publish this new third series consisting of 24 prints between November 1954 and September 1956, working closely with Wada as they did for the first two series.

One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It portrays Ainu hunters chasing and harpooning sea otters. In the background we see foreign ships who contributed to the near decimation of the sea otter population in the Kuril Islands (Chishima.)
Records of the Ainu hunting sea otters go back to the 1500s. Traditionally the Ainu hunted sea otters with bow and arrow, leister, and harpoon. Starting in the 1870s, at about the time this print was published, it was reported that most of the hunting was being done by foreign vessels and by 1897 a British sea captain reported that “sea-otter hunting on the Kurils are practically no longer worth considering…” due to their declining numbers. - Source: Notes on the Kuril Islands, Captain H. J. Snow, John Murray, 1897, p. 88.

Shipping Ice from Hakodate, Hokkaidō (北海道函館氷輸出之図 Hokkaidō Hakodate kōri yushutsu no zu)
Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)

One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.  It portrays people in Western-style garments cutting ice from the moat around Goryōkaku fort near Hakodate on the island of Hokkaidō, from where it was shipped, insulated with sawdust, to Yokohama, Tokyo and other southern destinations.  The ice would be held in storage until the summer months when it would fetch the highest prices. Production and transportation of natural water ice first succeeded in 1869.
Hakodate, located on Japan’s northernmost island of Hokkaidō, developed as a port town for trade with foreign countries at the end of the 19th century. From December 4, 1868 to June 27, 1869 the Goryōkaku fort was the site of the Battle of Hakodate fought between the remnants of the Tokugawa shogunate army, consolidated into the armed forces of the rebel Ezo Republic, and the armies of the newly formed Imperial government. This was the final battle in the Boshin War.

One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting the harvesting of kudzu (Japanese arrowroot or pueraria) root its being processed into powder. Yamato Province (大和国,Yamato no Kuni) was a province of Japan, located in Kinai, corresponding to present-day Nara Prefecture in Honshū.
"Young shoots from this abundant plant are boiled in an iron kettle in pieces 1 m. long, and then submitted to longer soaking in running water, till their bast becomes loose, when it is stripped off by hand. To bleach, soften, and divide its fibres, it is pounded and treated with water, and otherwise manipulated. When finished, the fibres are tolerably firm and white, like hemp-bast. They are used for the woof of several kinds of cloth, but only to a very limited extent." - Source: The Industries of Japan: Together with an Account of its Agriculture, Forestry, Arts and Commerce, Johannes Justus Rein, A. C. Armstrong & Son, 1889, p. 169.
As with this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. Ennosuke in the role of the Exiled King and Tōzō in the role of the Warrior Priest Kōku (猿之助 流離王 東蔵 好苦梵士)
August 1, 1915 - 大正四年八月一日 發行 as printed on cover of Shin Nigao v. 1, no. 3.

The actors Ichikawa Ennosuke II in the role of the exiled king and Nakamura Tōzō II as the warrior priest Kōku in the play Washimo Shiranai わしも知らない staged at tje Gekijō, Tokyo on June 28, 1915. One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. In both the top and bottom scenes Kyōsai portrays a husband dominated by his wife. In the top scene, a wife sits on her husband smoking a pipe, while her husband holds a tabakobon (tobacco tray) for her comfort. In the bottom print, a wife is putting mud on her husband's face to keep him from seeing her lover hiding behind a hanging kimono, to whom she hands a love letter.

Kasumi-ami 霞網 are stationary mist nets perfected for bird trapping in Japan in the late 1800s. Originally made of cotton or silk thread, modern mist nets are constructed of black nylon. Mist nets are firmly suspended end-to-end from bamboo, metal, or fiberglass poles, typically in parallel or angled arrays. Nets are placed in areas that are likely to attract feeding migrants, and in many instances raptors are attracted to the nets by already-captured passerines. - Source: Migrating Raptors of the World: Their Ecology and Conservation, Keith L. Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the upper left panel, playing the role of Teruhi no Miko in the kabuki play Uwanari. He wears a white hannya mask, denoting a vengeful female spirit of aristocratic background. Below Danjūrō is an unidentified actor playing the role of Kishō 吉聖.
The play Uwanari is variously translated as “The Mistress,” “The Second Wife,"“Jealousy,” and “Ambush of the Second Wife.” Uwanari was originally staged in 1699. While the original script has been lost, the play was re-written and re-staged in 1936.
Uwanari, which means “second wife” and “jealousy”, is a torrid tale of jealousy, hate, and love. In it, a man divorces his wife and marries another woman. But while the newlyweds enjoy marital bliss, the jilted wife fumes, and plots her revenge on her ex-husband and the woman who replaced her. Passions will flare and dark schemes will bloom in this in riveting play, all told through impassioned dance.[1]
"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[2]
The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

c. 1950s - the Adachi Institute who produced this series of experimental bunraku prints for Kiyoshi dates them to around "late Showa 20s".

In a January 2023 email in response to collector Jon Lipka's inquiry about this little known series of bunraku prints, Koko Nakayama of the Adachi Institute of Woodcut Prints wrote, "Adachi produced the Bunraku series of Kiyoshi Saito around the 50s (late Showa 20s). And the red small stamp on the back is ours. It was commission work just for the production, so we did not sell them. They were printed on the dyed in black non washi paper. It is quite an unusual production method for us, but it seems that we were asked to try it that way. Instead of printing with watercolors and letting them soak in the fibers of the washi paper, only this series was printed to let the colors sit on the paper with different types of paints, which creates the thick texture of the print as you mentioned. The black area we see underneath the other colors is the color of the dyed paper. It was ordered by either artist, Kiyoshi Saito or his publisher. After this series, we produced the other series (Children), but they were printed with a standard ukiyo-e style woodcut printing method."

June 1895 (Meiji 28, 6th month) - date appearing in the left margin of other impressions has been trimmed from this print

One of two known prints in the series Selections from Japanese History, issued by the little-known publisher Yazawa Hisakichi 矢沢久吉. This triptych pictures the tale of a woodcutter from Mino whose filial piety brought about a visit by the Empress Gensho 元正天皇 (reign 715-724). On the left we see the woodcutter and his father in front of Yōrō Falls paying reverence to the Empress in her palanquin who has come to see the reported miracle of the falls' water turning into sake.
As told in the Zenken kojitsu 前賢故実, during the 8th century a poor woodcutter went to the forest for firewood to warm his sick father. While searching, he came upon a waterfall whose water magically turned into sake. Filling his gourd he returns home to his ailing father who drinks the sake and miraculously recovers.
Hearing about this miracle, Empress Gensho visited the waterfall herself and determined that the miracle was a reward for the filial piety of the woodcutter. In honor of this miracle the Empress renamed the year of her reign "Yōrō", for the location of the waterfall.

The top portion of the print parodies the tale in which the bodhisattva Samantabhadra (Fugen), the protector of the Lotus Sutra, takes the guise of the courtesan Eguchi and offers shelter to a travelling monk. The bottom portion of the print, showing a lotus coming out of the mouth of courtesan, parodies the saying "a lotus in the mud", meaning that although the lotus grows in the mud, it is pure, the quintessential flower for Buddhists, as is the courtesan who tries to keep her heart pure although she is in a house of prostitution.
These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

In this print a raucous group of children are painting the belly of Hotei, the god of happiness. It is one of forty prints (chūban size) which make up the series Sketches by Yoshitoshi (Yoshitoshi ryakuga). The series consists of forty humorous subjects originally printed in pairs on an ōban size sheet.
Lea Baten in Playthings and Pastimes in Japanese Prints provides us with the following description of this print:
"[C]hildren painting Hotei’s belly to look like a giant mochi cake. Hotei, one of the seven gods of good luck, is the Japanese god of happiness, for in his huge sack he carries toys and treasures for the flocks of children who swarm around him everywhere. He is very tolerant and allows the boisterous bevy many liberties, while pondering sleepily and not too seriously on the deterioration of today’s morals. Here, after having received paint and paintbrush, a mischievous youngster is trying out his artistic talents on Hotei’s immense hairy stomach to the joy of the others who are accompanying his efforts with jumping, laughter, and brandishing toys. A plum blossom and a pine needle adorn the patient Hotei’s grotesque belly, which is being blown up through a natural channel, to put it euphemistically, by a daring juvenile delinquent with a long bamboo pipe." - Source: Playthings and Pastimes in Japanese Prints, Lea Baten,Weatherhill, 1995, p. 110-112.

This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. The printer, Yoneda Minoru, has employed Sasajima's takuzuri technique, employed on the original print, of forcing paper into a deep-cut block with a press and dabbing the raised areas with an ink saturated pad giving the print a sculpted three-dimensional appearance.

Hasegawa Sadanobu III 三代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu III 三代 小信 ) (1881-1963)

An illustration of the stage set for the opening scene of Act III “Tearing the Carriage Apart” in the play Sugawara Denju Tenarai Kagami [Sugawara and the Secrets of Calligraphy]. In this set an ox drawn carriage sits in front of Yoshida Shrine in Kyoto. Sakuramaru and Umeōmaru will battle their blood triplet brother Matsuōmaru over control of the carriage carrying Great Minister Shihei and the carriage and its axle will be reduced to mangled splinters.
The play is one of the “Three Masterpieces” of the puppet theater along with Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura and Kanadehon Chūshingura. It was written in 1746 by Namiki Sōsuke (Senryū) (1695-1751), Miyoshi Shōraku(1696-1772) and Takeda Koizumo (Izumo II) (1691–1756).
A later edition, post-WWII, print by Uchida Publishing issued without the tissue overlay present in the original edition.
The Illustrated Collection of Famous Japanese Puppets of the Osaka Bunrakuza
The Illustrated Collection of Famous Japanese Puppets of the Osaka Bunrakuza consists of twelve sets of prints each set depicting a specific play in the bunraku repertory. Each set contains a stage set for the specific play along with three prints of puppet characters appearing in the play and an explanatory sheet, for a total of forty-eight color woodblock prints and twelve monochrome explanatory sheets. All of the plays pictured were performed at the Bunraku Theater (Bunraku-za) located within the Goryō Shrine compound in Osaka. The Goryō Bunraku-za burned down in November 1926 after what has been described as "an extremely difficult managerial era" and "lost interest" by the public in the late Taishō era. It is unknown what role, if any, the management of the Goryō Bunraku-za may have played in the formulation and issuance of this print series in their efforts to revitalize the theater.

One of a number of posthumous prints created from Yumeji's illustrations by the Tokyo-based publisher Katō Junji. This print was released as part of the series Yumeji Masterpieces. This design was originally made for the 1917 cover of the musical score for Matoori Nagayo's "Rantō Kōta" (Song of the Lantern), published by Senow Ongaku Shuppansha.
"This woodblock print exemplifies Yumeji's lifelong interest in the exotic and foreign, as manifest in the recurring imagery of port cities. Here, a woman dressed in a vivid red kimono with shibari-dyed patterns and floral motifs casually plays a shamisen. A large paper lantern hangs behind here, with a view of the bay in the distance."[1]
"The majority of Yumeji’s woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934. The publisher who was instrumental in having Yumeji’s work recognized was the Tokyo-based Katō Junji (1885-1961). During the late 1930s and early 1940s, Katō and his team of artisan block-cutters and printers at the Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō) reused and recalled numerous famous paintings, music scores and watercolours for series of prints and postcards.
"The thirty woodblock prints in this set are a selection of the most popular cover designs from the over 270 that the artist produced of Seno music scores. Katō Junji personally compiled the set and it reflects what he believed was representative of Yumeji’s artistic diversity, ranging from the portrayal of beautiful women and landscapes to his fascination with Western artistic styles."[2]

One of at least fifteen prints from Saitō that depict maiko (Kyoto apprentice geisha) in various poses and from various angles. The first maiko print appeared in 1959 and they continued into the 1960s and, possibly, into the early 1970s. This print is from an unnumbered (open) edition and is not dated, but is likely from the late 1960s or early 1970s. The print is also seen with the artist's signature in white ink rather than black ink, as on this collection's print.
As with many of his prints, Saitō makes brilliant use of the natural grain of the woodblock. Melanie C. Gibb comments on Saitō's use of woodblock grain in the catalog of the exhibition Revisiting Modern Japanese Prints" as follows:
"He often began the carving process with a solid piece of katsura or plywood while later executing large areas of his designs with mokumezuri, or grain printing. This natural texture, exposed by scouring out the soft surface of the grain, is beautifully applied in the print Maiko, as seen in the large flat area of obi fabric which beautifully undulates against the curvilinear form of the geisha-in-training."

Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publisher's who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (DoiHangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

A small format woodblock reproduction, mounted on a greeting card, after Kitagawa Utamaro's 1801 nighttime depiction of two geisha and a porter in the driving wind and rain. There are many small woodblock reproductions derived from Utagawa's original print which can be seen in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. The original design was modified at some point, likely in early to mid 20th century, to add Utamaro's signature in the lower right corner of the image, which is not present on the original print, and to make color and other changes to the design. The earliest known small reproduction, similar to this collection's print, was shown in the catalog of the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō in 1938.

One of at least 83 small format prints, often referred to as "postcard size" prints, designed by Hasui for the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō (1885-1962). This image of Kyoto's Golden Pavilion (Kinkakuji) in snow has been often reproduced by other publishers without credit to the artist. (See IHL.0653, IHL.1424 and IHL.1668 for examples of prints very similar in design to Hasui's.) The publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō became so upset by these copies of original designs by Hasui and several other artists he published that he included the following warning in his 1936 catalogue titled, " Catalogue of Wood-Cut Colour Prints of S. Watanabe, S. Watanabe, 1936" :
"In case any picture already issued reproduced or copied by the third person without permission, he will be sued and judged as a violation of copyright, that is, as the infringement of property right.
"There had been examples that a few pictures issued by my shop were reproduced or copied without permission previous to the Great Earthquake disaster [1923] and after it. On each occasion the violator had to pay damages and to write letters of apology.”
This collection's print was originally tipped into the 1936 Watanabe sales catalog titled Catalogue of Wood-cut Color Prints, of S. Watanabe, p. 41, catalogue No. 896, and then removed. On p. 38 of that catalog the print is titled as "Snow scenery at Kinkakuji (Golden Temple)." Postcard size prints were first offered in Watanabe's 1931 sales catalog.
From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

License to publish March 1, 1882 - 明治十五年三日一日板權免許 as printed in volume two's colophon.

In this print, one of three color prints in Volume 2 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays Kusonoki's parting speech to his son at Sakura Station on his way to the Battle of Minatogawa, telling his eleven year old son Masatsura "I feel this is the last time I will see your face in this life." He orders him to return home to Kawachi to continue the family line and to support the emperor until death, ending by saying "This will be your most important filial duty to me." The Decorum of Gekiketsu (郤缼の禮)

In this print, one two color prints in Volume 3 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays the minister of state during China's Spring and Autumn Era (770-476 BC) as he observes the poor farmer Xi Que (Gekiketsu in Japanese) and his wife treating each other with great respect, as if they were each other's guest. When the minister told the king, the king appointed Xi Que to an important position in the state of Jin. Xi Que would go on to successively higher positions. For the other color print in this volume see IHL.1540a.

Published July 1884 - 明治十七年七月出版 as printed in volume 5's colophon publication

In this print, one two color prints in Volume 4 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays the samurai and Christian convert Kuroda Jusoi (1546-1604) who was known for his frugality and his generosity. Here he has instructed his servant to remove the flesh from some tai he had been sent as a present and make soup of the bones for he and his guests, who had borrowed money from him. His guests seeing this severe economy worried that they would be charged high interest on their loan but Kuroda would not even take the principal. The print's large cartouche provides an explanation suitable for a child of elementary school age to understand. For the other color print in this volume see IHL.1541b.

The commentary originally accompanying this post-war second edition (originally print number 13 in the series) reads "A Story-teller (Kamishibai) - When he finds a good place for his business on the street, he stops and makes ready the pictures illustrating his stories in the case on his bicycle. A pictorial story-teller is a Pied-piper [sic] of Hamelin in Japan, and the children are like the rats running after the piper."
The commentary for this post-war edition leaves out the following which was included in the commentary to the first edition issued during the Pacific War. "It is indeed natural that the authorities have recently been making efforts to lead in the right direction this business [the picture card show] that may well be employed as a valuable organ to … develop their [children’s] thought."

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2]

[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

Sponsored by the Votive Women's Association, print 18, Lake Hamana and  Futaminoura (納札 婦人會 催主, 十八・濱各湖・二見浦)

One of a set of at least eighteen votive prints (nōsatsu 納札 or senjafuda 千社札) picturing various scenic places designed by the painter Takeda Keihō, a student of the Meiji era nihonga painter and woodblock designer Mizuno Toshikata (1866-1908) for an unknown women's votive association. Over the years votive temple offerings evolved from small wood plaques, to small paper slips bearing the names of pilgrims, attached by pilgrims to Buddhist and Shinto shrine buildings, to woodblock printed designs called kōkanfuda (交換札), to be shared among members of votive associations (nōsatsukai) at nōsatsu exchange meetings. The various motifs of kōkanfuda were inspired by nishiki-e themes: kabuki actors, famous landscapes, scenes from popular literature, and legendary and mythical figures.
This print provides views of Lake Hamana and Meoto Iwa (Wedded Rocks) at Futaminoura.

A view of the dam along the Hollyhock Slope in Minoato-ku. According to Edo Meisho Zue, a gazetteer of Edo published in the 1810s, "Beside the dam on the other side of the corner checkpoint, which is on the north side of the reservoir, is an area which has been planted with aoi, hollyhocks. This area is called Hollyhock Hill, and the slope that runs downwards to the east from here is called Aoizaka, Hollyhock Slope." The tiled hut in the foreground and the other tiled hut on the hill to the left seem to be the corner checkpoints, or tsujibansho, mentioned in the gazetteer. These checkpoints were set up in this area where samurai and noblemen resided to maintain surveillance and keep order. The road sloping to the left is probably Aoizaka; the reservoir and the dam are on the right.
As with many of Hiroshige II's prints, the prints comprising the series Forty-Eight Famous Views of Edo borrowed from the designs of his teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I.

One of Rei's semi-abstract landscapes created from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s. "The texture of the woodblock itself creates dappled tones and fragile shades. The works are light, yet the source of the light is hidden behind fences and arches. It is a light defined by shadows, creating a mood of timeless suspension.
"Leafless branches cast foreground shadows, mysteriously real and abstract, stark and delicate. The texture of the block, structural unity of the geometric ground figures, subdued coloration and shading, and magical, waving forms together create a locus, a place that is both definite and infinite, haunting and unassuming, vague and too vivid to be mere fantasy." - Source: Who's Who in Modern Japanese Prints, Francis Blakemore, Weatherhill, 1975, p. 247.

Kitaoka's rendering of Kintai-bashi with Iwakuni Castle atop Mt. Yokoyama in the background.
“Kintaibashi is located on the foot of Mt.Yokoyama, at the top of which lies Iwakuni Castle. After Iwakuni Castle was completed in 1608 by Kikkawa Hiroie, the first lord of Iwakuni Domain, a series of wooden bridges were built. However, most of them were destroyed by floods several times before the construction of the iconic Kintaibashi in 1673. New stone piers replaced the old wooden ones.
"Though thought to be flood-proof; the bridge was destroyed by a flood the next year. As a result, the stone piers were redesigned for greater strength, and a special tax was created to maintain the bridge. This maintenance involved periodic rebuilding of the bridge: every 20 years for 3 spans in the middle, every 40 years for 2 spans connecting to the riverside.
"Consequently, the bridge remained undestroyed for 276 years, until washed away again by flooding from typhoon ‘Kijia’ in 1950. It had been in a weakened state at the time, due to the fact that the Japanese had stopped maintaining the bridge during World War II, and that the year before the typhoon, a large amount of gravel was taken by the US military forces from the river around the bridge to expand the US Marine Corps Air Station in Iwakuni, strengthening the flow of the river.
"In 1953, the bridge was reconstructed similarly to the original, using metal nails made from the same tatara iron as the Katana to increase its durability. Between 2001 and 2004, all five bridge girders were restored for the first time in 50 years." Source: website of oldtokyo.com http://www.oldtokyo.com/kintaibashi-iwakuni-c-1910/ [accessed 8-17-23]

One of fifteen prints from the 1945 series Scenes of Last Tokyo. This print was one of eight designs for the series which originally appeared in the 1929-1932 series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). This 1945 print was made from recut blocks. It is one of two designs that Hiratsuka contributed to Scenes of Last Tokyo, the publication of which was orchestrated by Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955).
The building in the centre is the main office of Asahi Shimbun, one of Japan's biggest newspapers, completed in 1927. The bridge was demolished in 1957, and the canal filled in.

SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. - Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

Picturing a tiger with his prey, a parrot, in his mouth, and representing the third sign of the zodiac, this print was published on January 1, 1903, as dated in its left margin. Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals, the series which this print is a part of, was originally issued c. 1901, again in 1903 and then reissued by Unsōdō Publishing several times into the early 1940s. As this print has a centerfold, it may have been issued as part of a folding album with the other eleven prints representing the animals in the zodiac, or it may have been issued as a stand-alone print.
Each of the prints in Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals is essentially a woodblock facsimile of what must have been an original watercolor created by Seihō, a nihonga, Maruyama-Shijō school painter. In describing an earlier book of prints by the artist, also published by Unsōdō Publishing, Jack Hillier notes that the Meiji printmakers responded to the challenge of reproducing Seihō's watercolors, with "marvelous interpretive skills" and goes on to say “There is, in truth, a complete abnegation of the medium qua woodcut; its own virtues of bold line and flat wash are sacrificed in the cause of a facsimile rendering of a water-colour: this was a fundamental change in technique which led to incredible feats of reproduction…”

Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)

The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III, a disciple of the great Utagawa Hiroshige I (1797-1858), created these sketches (manga) in 1879, which were arranged three, four or five to a single sheet as a harimaze-e. Titled "Sketches by Ryūsai," Ryūsai being an artist name (gō) of Hiroshige III, they were very much in the tradition of his master Hiroshige I, who is sometimes credited as the inventor of the print genre harimaze, which can be literally translated as "paste and mix pictures" and is commonly translated as "cut-out pictures."
The height of their popularity was in the mid-1800s and these inexpensive prints were purchased and then often cut-apart and pasted onto Japanese screens or into scrapbooks. Harimazi-e could include the work of multiple artists or just a single artist, as in the case of these harimaze-e. For other examples of harimazi-e in this collection see Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889) and his works from the series Kyōsai Manga.

Sound of the Wind (風のひびき Kaze no hibiki )

Rei continued to pursue in this 1991 work an earlier style described by Francis Blakemore in 1975 as follows:
"The texture of the woodblock itself creates dappled tones and fragile shades. The works are light, yet the source of the light is hidden behind fences and arches. It is a light defined by shadows, creating a mood of timeless suspension.
"Leafless branches cast foreground shadows, mysteriously real and abstract, stark and delicate. The texture of the block, structural unity of the geometric ground figures, subdued coloration and shading, and magical, waving forms together create a locus, a place that is both definite and infinite, haunting and unassuming, vague and too vivid to be mere fantasy." - Source: Who's Who in Modern Japanese Prints, Francis Blakemore, Weatherhill, 1975, p. 247.

He therefore waits for her to arrive, and then begins to cross the river. On the way, the traveller asks the reason for the crowd of people on the other bank. The boatman tells him that they are there to perform a mass for a boy of about eleven years of age, the son of one Yoshida from the capital, who died there a year ago after being taken from his home. At this, the woman weeps bitterly, and reveals that the boy was the son she is seeking. The ferryman takes her to the grave and when they recite prayers there, the boy's voice is heard. The mother prays again and her son appears to her. But when she reaches out for him he is no longer there, and with the coming of dawn he disappears again forever." - source: A Guide to No, P.G. Kitaoka depicts the lower level gardens and Ogonchi Pond at Kokedera (Moss Temple), also known as Saihoji.
Saihoji Temple belongs to the Rinzai school of Japanese Buddhism. In 1994 the site was registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The gardens built by Muso Soseki (a nationally designated scenic and historic site) consist of an upper level of dry karesansui-style rock arrangements and a lower level built around Ogonchi Pond, which is shaped like the Chinese character meaning "heart." Blanketed by more than 120 species of moss, the temple is popularly and affectionately known as Kokedera ("Moss Temple").

Volume 6 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895.  Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

Annual Events of the Edo Theatre (大江戸しばゐねんぢうぎやうじ Ō-Edo shibai nenjū-gyōji)
Originally 1897. The date of this second edition print, is unknown.

This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts a soba (buckwheat noodle) stand in front of the Ichimuraza Theater, one of the three officially recognized Kabuki theaters of Edo. The word "nihachi" (二八, literally 'two-eight'), written on the noodle stand, came from the noodles that cost sixteen (two times eight) mon a bowl and also from the proportion of 20 parts udon flour to 80 parts soba flour.
"With the excitement of the experience still in the air, fellow theatre aficionados might pass time after the performance exchanging opinions about what they had seen, as depicted in this print of men standing around talking in front of the theatre while slurping noodles from a food cart. Collecting this gossip was useful to the theatres. Spies would be sent out to listen in, and according to what they heard, acts might be replaced or play content might otherwise be modified. This print depicts a time before the three licensed Edo theatres (Edo sanza) were forced to move to Saruwaka-chō in Asakusa as a result of the Tenpō Reforms (1841-1843)." Source: Art Research Center, Ritsumeikan University https://www.arc.ritsumei.ac.jp/lib/vm/kabuki2015_e/2015/11/post-17.html [accessed 8-17-23]

Igawa Sengai is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to popular magazines such as Kingu (King), Fujin gahō (Graphic Magazine for Women) and Kōdan Kurabu (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) "A Pair of Pines" (Hiyoku no matsu), "Lady Shizuka" (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and "The Gold Demon" (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).
This untitled offset-printed color lithograph bijin kuchi-e (frontispiece illustrations of beautiful women) with its characteristic tri-fold, appeared in an unknown magazine.

THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E
The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

One of a number of posthumous prints created from Yumeji's illustrations by the Tokyo-based publisher Katō Junji. This print was released as part of the series Yumeji Masterpieces. This design was originally created for the 1926 cover of the musical score for Joseph Mazzinghi's "Ye Shepherds Tell Me" (The Wreath. A Pastoral Glee for Three Voices), published by Senow Ongaku Shuppansha.
"The prints in Yumeji Masterpieces highlight Yumeji's skillful treatment of the landscape genre. Tranquil, bucolic scenes such as this print, illustrating a hamlet nestled along a bay, were a frequent theme in Yumeji's art, and it could be conjectured that it conveyed a sense of nostalgia for his native Okayama or the port city of Kobe where he briefly spent time during his childhood."[1]
"The majority of Yumeji’s woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934. The publisher who was instrumental in having Yumeji’s work recognized was the Tokyo-based Katō Junji (1885-1961). During the late 1930s and early 1940s, Katō and his team of artisan block-cutters and printers at the Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō) reused and recalled numerous famous paintings, music scores and watercolours for series of prints and postcards.
"The thirty woodblock prints in this set are a selection of the most popular cover designs from the over 270 that the artist produced of Seno music scores. Katō Junji personally compiled the set and it reflects what he believed was representative of Yumeji’s artistic diversity, ranging from the portrayal of beautiful women and landscapes to his fascination with Western artistic styles."[2]
For another impression of this print see IHL.1575 printed on a lighter weight paper that appears to be a later edition than this impression.

Hagiwara’s Thirty-Six Fujis series is the artist’s only excursion into landscape. It is his homage to the sacred mountain and to past ukiyo-e artists, such as Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1848) and Utagawa Hiroshige (1797–1858). Living near Mount Fuji, Hagiwara gathered his impressions of the mountain for over fifteen years before beginning work on this series. Toward the end of the project he wrote: “Just when I think I have grasped [Fuji], it slips through my hands. Let's pick up this ‘slippery Fuji’ and keep on going.” Hagiwara captures a view of Fuji from the town of Ōhara on a spring morning, during the annual burning of grasslands (noyaki) on the northern foot of the mountain.

Volume 3 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895. Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

One of many chromolithograph bijin kuchi-e created for popular magazines by Morita, a yōga-trained (western style) artist who worked as a reporter, illustrator and art director. He contributed illustrations to numerous popular magazines in the late Meiji and Taishō era. His illustrations were primarily of the bijinga genre and they appeared in mass culture magazines such as Kōdan Kurabo, Kōdan zasshi, Fujokai, Jogaku sekai and in serialized novels. It is reported that his illustrations for a serialized novel appearing in the Yomiuri shinbun in 1921 were the first such illustrations to actually identify the illustrator by name.

THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E
The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

One of eight prints, seven of which are woodblock prints, appearing in the 1920 "pocket edition" (shukusatsu 縮刷), published by Shunyōdō 春葉堂, of The Gold Demon 金色夜叉 by the popular novelist and poet Ozaki Kōyō 尾崎紅葉 (1868-1903).
Sengai's illustration is that of the character Sayama Motosuke, the true love of O’Shizu (really Aiko of the Kashiwaya geisha house), who makes a suicide pact with her. Pictured are the rings they exchanged the night of their planned suicide, which was interrupted by the novel's main character, Kan’ichi.
For other prints appearing in the novel see IHL.1642, IHL. 1643 and IHL.1644.
Igawa Sengai is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to such popular magazines such as Kingu (King), Fujin gahō (Graphic Magazine for Women) and Kōdan Kurabu (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) A Pair of Pines (Hiyoku no matsu), Lady Shizuka (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and The Gold Demon (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).

The print depicts the ghost of the poet Narihira at Ōhara viewing the cherry blossoms, in a scene from the play Oshio by the playwright Komparu Zenchiku (1405-c. 1470).
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 81, cat. 26.) - A man (waki) and his two companions (wakizure) view the famous cherry blossoms at Ōhara, also known as Oshio, a hill to the southwest of Kyoto. They meet an old man (shite), who is obviously a person of elegant taste. He tells them stories about the place and recites poems written by the famous Heian courtier Ariwara no Narihira when he visited the spot. In the second part of the play, the old man now reappears as Narihira, riding in a vehicle from which to view the flowers. He recites some of his poems, dances in the moonlight, and then vanishes at dawn.
In the print, Narihira stands in a flower-viewing vehicle and observes the cherry blossoms.
The square inset in the upper right-hand corner includes part of a famous waka poem on the vicissitudes of love written by Narihira, which the shite delivers:
Is not the moon the same?
The spring
Not the spring of old?
Only this body of mine
Is the same body. . .


Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

The print depicts the climatic scene in the play Mochizuki sometimes attributed to the playwright Sa-ami (15th c.). "Thirteen years ago, the evil Mochizuki no Akinaga had killed Yasuda no Tomoharu. Now Mochizuki is staying at an inn, having just returned from Kyoto where he claimed Yasuda’s property. Unbeknownst to the murderer, the innkeeper Kozawa had been a retainer of Yasuda. Also at the inn are Yasuda’s widow and son. The three plot revenge: they offer to entertain Mochizuki. While the widow sings, her son plays a drum and then dances. Kozawa appears dressed as a lion dancer and is able to approach and stab Mochizuki to death." - Source: Ruth Chandler Williamson Gallery, Scripps College http://web-kiosk.scrippscollege.edu/Obj21710?sid=83782&x=1666787 [accessed 8-17-23]

Print number thirteen (十三, as printed in the right margin) in the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi shiseki meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941, depicting the large plaza in which sits the shrine's first gate (Kashihara jingū daiichi torii). The obelisk to the right is engraved with the shrine's name 橿原神宮.
Kashihara jingū is a Shinto shrine located in the city of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture, Japan. The shrine's vast precincts cover an area of roughly 500,000 square meters. It was built in 1889 at the site of the Kashihara-gū where Japan's mythical first emperor, Emperor Jimmu, is said to have acceded to the throne on February 11, 660 BC.
The use of the word Yamato 大和 in the print's title references the national foundation story embodied by Emperor Jimmu and the Kigen 2600 celebrations, starting in 1940, that marked the mythical 2,600th anniversary of Japan's founding. These celebrations which were years in the planning, were used to build popular support for Japan's territorial ambitions. More than 12,000 events were held to commemorate the anniversary including the publishing of this print series. Commenting on the series the artist writes that his devotion to the sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the "dignity of the national polity," going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

SCENES OF SACRED AND HISTORIC PLACES and THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF KIGEN 2600
The print artist Tokuriki and the publisher Uchida created two series of prints to mark Kigen 2600, or the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. The first, a paean to Mount Fuji, a sacred site of pilgrimage and worship, titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, harkened back to Hokusai’s famous 1831 series of the same name. The second series, Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, capitalized on the nationalist ideology that Japan was a divine land, presenting overtly nationalistic landscapes including shrines, temples, castles, places associated with the divine origins of Japan, Meiji era history and samurai culture.

In his commentary on the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, the artist wrote that his devotion to these sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the dignity of the national polity, going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

Usa Shrine 宇佐神宮 (Usa jingū]

Print number nineteen (十九, as printed in the right margin) in the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941. Tokuriki gives us a view of the sacred bridge [神橋 shinkyō], leading to the main entrance of the shrine, on a moonlit evening.
The shrine was founded in Kyūshū during the Nara period. Ancient records place the foundation of Usa jingū in the Wadō era (708-714). A temple called Miroku-ji was built next to it in 779, making it what is believed to be the first shrine-temple (jingū-ji) ever. From 1871 through 1946, Usa was officially designated one of the Kanpei-taisha (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. The shrine is the main sanctum of over 40,000 hachiman shrine locations. The Emperor Ojin, who was deified as Hachiman-shin (the god of military power) and worshiped as the protective deity of the Imperial City, is enshrined in these shrines.

Linesmen installing electrical lines and transformers during the era when electrical power, its generation, transmission and distribution, were under state control. This print is number twenty-one in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures.
A translated version of the original Japanese language commentary accompanying this print reads, "Looking down from a high place upon the crowds of a busy city, the profession of the electrical linesman, always wearing blue and working beneath the blue sky, is a happy one. The difference between them is whether electricity runs through them or not.
"Tokyo is gradually becoming more distinguished, but I will not go into detail here about how it fills me with pride when I see the above ground utility poles standing closely together, which major cities in the west do not have."[1]

OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]

A helmsman and his wife ply their boat through a fast moving river, while their two children lounge on a plank in the boat. A more modern boat chugs along in the background. Along with the print title, this collection's print has the series title and the number of the print in the series printed within the image area. The vast majority of prints in the series carry the series title in the lower right margin, not within the image area, and not all prints show the series number on the print.
The commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "This is a scene still to be found on the Sumida River. Among the busy steam and motor boats, weaving up and down the stream, slowly move the man-propelled barges. The occupation of the river boatman, sharing his work with his wife, living day in and day out on the water, making one corner of his narrow boat his world and enjoying his family life there, is a rich possession, alleviating the bewilderment of dizzy modern life."

The Illustrated Collection of Famous Japanese Puppets of the Osaka Bunrakuza consists of twelve sets of prints each set depicting a specific play in the bunraku repertory. Each set contains a stage set for the specific play along with three prints of puppet characters appearing in the play and an explanatory sheet, for a total of forty-eight color woodblock prints and twelve monochrome explanatory sheets. All of the plays pictured were performed at the Bunraku Theater (Bunraku-za) located within the Goryō Shrine compound in Osaka. The Goryō Bunraku-za burned down in November 1926 after what has been described as "an extremely difficult managerial era" and "lost interest" by the public in the late Taishō era. Yumi yawata 弓八幡 (The Bow at the Hachiman Shrine)

The series was originally published between 1925 and 1930. In 1936 and again in 1937 it was republished (a "revised edition" 改版) under the title Nōga taikan: nōga nihyakuban ōzoroe (能畫大鑑 : 能畫貮百番大揃, Nōga taikan: 200 prints of Noh play), in which the prints were bound into a single volume. A specific publishing date for this print cannot be determined.

Play synopsis - Yumi Yawata is a two act play centering on a warrior’s bow wrapped in a brocade bag. The maejite, an old man, appears with the bow at the Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine in Kyoto and presents it to the waki, a retainer of the Ex-Emperor Gouda (1267-1324), to be offered up to His Majesty. As the shite explains: “Among the historical precedents of the land of China, brought to peaceful rule under the Zhou, one finds the precedent of wrapping one’s bow and arrows in a bag and shutting away one’s lance and shield. Accordingly, I have stuffed this bow into a bag and put my sword away in a box; these very actions are a sign of our lord’s age of great peace.” According to the recorded words of Zeami, the author of the play, the play was written “in honor of the inaugural celebration for the reign of the present shogun."

Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays), made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé.
"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

Print number fifty (五十, as printed in the right margin) of the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941. It is perhaps the ultimate nationalist print in the series, depicting Hakkō Ichiu Tower in Miyazaki erected in 1940 to commemorate the 2,600th anniversary of the mythical ascension of Japan's first emperor, Jimmu, on 11 February 660 BC.

SCENES OF SACRED AND HISTORIC PLACES and THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF KIGEN 2600
The print artist Tokuriki and the publisher Uchida created two series of prints to mark Kigen 2600, or the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. The first, a paean to Mount Fuji, a sacred site of pilgrimage and worship, titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, harkened back to Hokusai’s famous 1831 series of the same name. The second series, Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, capitalized on the nationalist ideology that Japan was a divine land, presenting overtly nationalistic landscapes including shrines, temples, castles, places associated with the divine origins of Japan, Meiji era history and samurai culture.
In his commentary on this series, the artist wrote that his devotion to these sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the dignity of the national polity, going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

Takemura & Co.) who targeted his work at a Western audience, specializing in, as printed on his business card, Christmas Cards, Japanese Old Colour Prints, Famous Modern Colour Prints and Water Colors.
The publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō became so upset by these copies of original designs by Hasui and several other artists he published that he included the following warning in his 1936 catalogue titled, "Catalogue of Wood-Cut Colour Prints of S. Watanabe, S. Watanabe, 1936" :
"In case any picture already issued reproduced or copied by the third person without permission, he will be sued and judged as a violation of copyright, that is, as the infringement of property right.
"There had been examples that a few pictures issued by my shop were reproduced or copied without permission previous to the Great Earthquake disaster [1923] and after it. On each occasion the violator had to pay damages and to write letters of apology.”
Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (Doi Hangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints).

One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print Fuji is barely visible from the rice planting area around Bentenjima. Three bi-planes along with four birds fly through the sky, while a traditionally dressed rice-farmer and old-fashioned fishing boats go about their business. Again, the artist juxtaposing the traditional with the modern.
The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[1]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, p. 53.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Published March 1904 (Meiji 37) - 明治丗七年三月 日 発行 as printed in publisher's "double-fish" cartouche.

As part of Japan's efforts to emulate Western institutions, the Japanese Red Cross was established in 1877 during the Seinan War (a.k.a. Satsuma Rebellion). By the time of the Sino-Japanese War [1894-1895], images of the Red Cross tending to fallen soldiers had become part of the standard iconography of the battlefield; the Japanese were to be seen as not only mighty but also magnanimous, as befitted an "enlightened" nation. Such descriptions would only proliferate during the Russo-Japanese War, with the Japanese Red Cross shown selflessly caring for Japanese and Russian wounded alike.[1]
In this print the magnanimity of the Japanese is driven home by the inset in the top of the center sheet showing "brutal Russian soldiers" 露國野蠻兵 tearing a child away from its mother. (For another print depicting the Japanese Red Cross in action on the battlefield see IHL.0104, The Humane Ambulance Corps of the Japanese Red Cross.)
A later state of this print added an English transcription, written in cursive, to the upper left hand corner of the left sheet reading "Japan Red Society Hospital treating the wounded in the Russo-Japanese war."

[1] A Much Recorded War: The Russo-Japanese War in History and Imagery, Fredrick A. Sharf, Anne Nishimura Morse, Sebastian Dobson, MFA Publications, 2005, p. 44.

One of at least six prints in a series depicting various aspects of Korean life. While published in the 1950s, the scenes are reminiscent of the time of the artist's residency in Korea from 1909 through the end of its colonization by Japan in 1945. In this idyllic scene, women are washing or carrying laundry. Isabella Bird, in writing about her visit to Korea at the end of the 19th century, painted a less idyllic picture, at least of clothes washing in Seoul, as follows:
"She washes in this foul river, in the pond of the Mulberry Palace, in every wet ditch, and outside the walls in the few streams which exist. Clothes are partially unpicked, boiled with lye three times, rolled into hard bundles, and pounded with heavy sticks on stones. After being dried they are beaten with wooden sticks on cylinders, till they attain a polish resembling dull satin. The women are slaves to the laundry, and the only sound which breaks the stillness of a Seoul night is the regular beat of their laundry sticks."

Pictured in this set of woodblock prints are the Buddhist and Shinto gods of wind, Fūjin 風神, and thunder, Raijin 雷神, whose names are written in calligraphic form on the cover print. All three prints were placed in an envelope with a label adhered to it noting that they were “not for sale.” These prints, designed by an unknown artist who signed his name 守拙 (Shusetsu?), were commissioned by a nōsatsukai (an association of nōsatsu, Japanese votive slips, devotees) and meant for distribution to members, hence they were“not for sale.” The names of the members of the nōsatsukai appear as small votive strips in the bottom portion of each print, 75 slips on each of the three prints. While the prints are undated, they are most likely a post-1950 production.

Sanomura and Mount Fuji (佐野村と富士)

One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print Fuji looms large behind the rice field and farmers in the foreground at work irrigating the rice field.
The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."
